extracted.intended_audience: science/medical journalists, health reporters, and anyone interested in newsroom-embargo practices
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles about handling journal embargoes, press privileges, and decisions to honor or break embargoes in science and medical reporting. Includes real-world examples (JAMA blacklists) and considerations about public interest, selective disclosure, and political use of embargoes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uphold embargoes to retain press privileges
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal editors and journals (e.g., JAMA) enforce embargoes and may revoke press privileges or blacklist journalists they believe broke an embargo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Pat had her JAMA press privileges revoked after JAMA told her she had broken the embargo; Adam was blacklisted after publishing about an embargoed JAMA study. Consequence: loss of embargoed material access; reporters should weigh the cost of losing direct embargoed access against other ways of reporting the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify whether an embargo was actually broken before judging
rubrics_metrics.description: Disputes arise over whether a reporter truly broke an embargo versus having independently obtained or reported on information from other sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pat claims she did not break the embargo because her reporting came from sources and pre-existing conversations; yet JAMA judged otherwise and revoked privileges. Journalists and editors should consider provenance of reporting and whether the embargo violation accusation is justified before accepting punitive measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize responsibility to readers when deciding to break an embargo
rubrics_metrics.description: A reporter's primary duty is to inform readers; this can justify breaking an embargo if public-interest reporting requires it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adam's stance: 'Who am I most responsible to?' — if informing readers requires discussing embargoed-but-broken information, he will do so and accept penalties. Use this as an ethical test: if embargo adherence conflicts with serving public interest, breaking may be defensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critically assess motives behind embargoes
rubrics_metrics.description: Many embargoes may be placed for political or self-serving reasons rather than purely scientific or public-interest ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pat: 'Most embargoes are placed for political or totally self-serving reasons.' Reporters should be skeptical of embargo timing and the motives (e.g., accommodating a press conference or political appearance) when evaluating the newsworthiness and fairness of embargoes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for and object to selective disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Selective disclosure — giving some parties access or allowing certain outlets earlier access — undermines the fairness of embargo systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: JAMA gave early access to a TV network before the embargo lifted; selective disclosure can create inequities (e.g., for trading on information) and is criticized by reporters like Adam. Reporters and editors should note when embargoed material is distributed unevenly and factor that into decisions about compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider market implications of embargoed scientific findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Embargoed medical research can move financial markets; journals may not consider or be responsible for market effects, but reporters should.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adam's example: a JAMA study depressed a company's stock; JAMA's spokeswoman said financial markets are not JAMA's concern. Guidance: financial journalists may need to publish earlier if embargoed findings materially affect investors and public markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate the news-management role of press releases and embargoes
rubrics_metrics.description: Embargoes and scheduled press conferences are often tools for managing how and when news is released, sometimes to serve institutional priorities rather than the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pat observed press conferences and embargoes scheduled to accommodate appearances by politicians or to allow institutions to control credit. Reporters should be aware of news-management motives and seek independent reporting rather than passively relaying embargoed materials that serve PR aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance reliance on embargoed journal material with independent reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal studies may not always be the most compelling or exclusive source; reporters can and should pursue other sources and reporting angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pat 'backed off writing JAMA studies' and found many studies were not the most compelling stories. Guidance: leave routine study summaries to wire services when appropriate and focus on original reporting, context, or investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess the value of embargoed access to your beat
rubrics_metrics.description: The practical worth of embargoed access varies by reporter; if embargoed material rarely yields market-moving or exclusive stories, losing access may be tolerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adam said he 'wasn't getting much value out of JAMA' and could count on few market-moving items. Reporters should evaluate whether maintaining embargo access provides sufficient professional benefit relative to editorial independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge that embargo systems can chill aggressive reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Embargo systems, and punitive measures like blacklisting, may make journalists more docile and less likely to dig independently, potentially harming important reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commentary: embargo enforcement could discourage enterprising reporters and reduce investigative coverage. Journalists and editors should be conscious of this risk and weigh institutional access against the need for adversarial reporting.
